sanctimonious

/sangk-tuh-MOH-nee-uhs/ - the stress falls on MOH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sanctimonious means showily virtuous in a hypocritical way.

Her sanctimonious post about 'a weekend unplugged' went up from her phone, followed by three reminders to like it.

Worked Example

Every morning Ted delivered a sanctimonious sermon on waste, inspecting the carpool's coffee cups for forbidden plastic. Then his own trunk popped open at the gas station, and out rolled a case of bottled water—yet by Tuesday the sermons had resumed, holier than ever.

Sanctimonious targets the performance of virtue: the display, the lecture, the halo polished in public. The plain word for the underlying gap is hypocrisy; sanctimonious describes how that gap sounds when it preaches.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

holier-than-thou: Holier-than-thou behavior is openly acting morally superior to everyone around — the raised eyebrow at your lunch, the sigh at your shortcuts. Sanctimonious adds a darker claim: the virtue on display is a performance the preacher does not live. A holier-than-thou scold may practice what she preaches; the sanctimonious one only performs.

preachy: Preachy is about delivery: moral advice pressed on people constantly and tediously, whether or not the preacher is sincere. Sanctimonious condemns the substance as well as the style — the showy virtue is false, a halo polished in public but not worn at home. A devoted coach can be preachy without ever being sanctimonious.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

humble: making no show of one's virtues

unassuming: quiet in manner, claiming no special credit

Where it sits · how far the display outruns real virtue — moralizing → self-righteous → sanctimonious

moralizing vs. sanctimonious: Moralizing lectures readily about right and wrong, but the lecturer may be sincere and even live by it; sanctimonious has left sincerity behind.

self-righteous vs. sanctimonious: Self-righteous is the belief in one's own superior virtue; sanctimonious goes one rung further—wearing that virtue as a public costume, usually one the wearer doesn't live in.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sanct

Root — sanct: holy, sacred

Suffix — -imoni

Suffix — -imoni: state or condition (from Latin -monia)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Sanct (holy) + -imoni (state of) + -ous (full of) = full of the state of holiness. Latin sanctimonia began as a compliment—genuine sacredness. English kept the word but curdled it: by Shakespeare's day sanctimonious already meant holiness worn for show, and the sneer has never washed out.

Use the root in a new word: sanctuary

Use the root in a new word: sanctuary: The wildlife sanctuary gives injured hawks a protected place to heal.

Word Choice

disapproving / literary

Sanctimonious is never a compliment: it accuses someone of performing virtue—preaching, sighing, polishing a halo—without living it. Hypocrisy, its partner in this unit, names the underlying gap between the preaching and the conduct; sanctimonious describes the showy lecture itself. A sincere moralizer may be tiresome, but only the false show earns sanctimonious.
